title: Making a picture in your head while you read
examples: How do I picture a story in my head?
How can I understand what I read?

faq.q: How do I make a picture in my head?
faq.a: Read a sentence, then stop and close your eyes. Think: what would this look like? Imagine the colours, the people and the place.
Think about who is there, where they are, the colours, the sounds and even the smells. The more details, the brighter your picture.
Change your picture to match! Good readers keep updating the film in their heads as they read.
asks: What happens when the story changes?

faq.q: Why does picturing help me read?
faq.a: Making a picture helps you understand what is happening and remember it later. Words turn into a film you can replay.

faq.q: What if I cannot make a picture in my head?
faq.a: That is okay, every mind works differently. You can draw a quick picture on paper instead, or talk about what is happening with a grown-up.
asks: I cannot see pictures in my head

facts: Making pictures in your mind while you read is called visualising.
Many reading teachers teach visualising as a way to understand and remember stories.

quiz.say: What should Ama do when the story changes?
quiz.show: The story changes. What should Ama do?
quiz.why: She changes her picture so it matches the story.

wrong.1: The old picture would not match the story any more.
wrong.2: No need to stop. Just change the picture and read on.

quiz.say: Which is a good detail to add to your picture?
quiz.show: A good detail for your picture?
quiz.why: The colour of the kite is part of the story, so it makes your picture brighter.

wrong.1: Your lunch is not in the story.
wrong.2: Your favourite number is not part of the story.
